newsitem.title: USA: Clinton regrets arms dealer's White House visit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton regrets arms dealer's White House visit.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday he regretted a Chinese arms dealer's involvement in a campaign fundraising event, and promised better screening of visitors to the White House in the future.

"I'm disappointed that it happened. It was clearly inappropriate," Clinton said when asked at a news conference why Wang Jun, who heads a weapons trading firm owned by the Chinese government, had been to the White House last February for a small private coffee with the president.

Wang's presence at a gathering designed to give Clinton a chance to meet about a dozen big political donors is the latest of a series of campaign fundraising embarrassments that have beset the president and the Democratic Party for weeks.

The controversy has led a Justice Department task force looking into how Clinton raised tens of millions of dollars for his re-election drive to issue wide-ranging subpoenas to the White House and the Democratic National Committee.
The subpoenas demand production of all records related to the fundraising activities of the president and his party.
Wang's visit occurred at a time of heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing over Chinese arms sales to Iran and Pakistan.

The visit was arranged by Charles Yah Lin Trie, an Asian-American businessman who has known Clinton for 20 years. Trie has been under fire for soliciting $640,000 in questionable donations for the legal defence fund of Clinton and his wife Hillary, money later returned by fund trustees.

"I have no recollection of meeting him (Wang)," Clinton said. "I'm not sure he ever said anything and I can tell you for sure nothing inappropriate came from it in terms of any governmental action on my part."

"You know, thousands of people come in and out of the larger White House office complex all the time. But we have to develop some way of screening them," the president added. "We must have a better screening system. We will have."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had asked outgoing White House chief of staff Leon Panetta to see to it that more "attention and care" is paid to the makeup of White House guest lists. He described Clinton as "displeased" with the recent developments surrounding Trie.

"We've seen now a series of things that suggest that some people brought friends or associates here with them to the White House for purposes that might not be consistent with what the president would expect of those who are guests," he said.

McCurry said no screening system was completely foolproof however, and reminded reporters, many of whom attended White House Christmas parties this week, that their guests were not subjected to background checks.
